name: Identifying A Driver By Full Name, Introduction Website Or Reference Name
description: A driver is identified by drivers.forename and drivers.surname together, as two columns in that order, because neither alone says who the person is. Two further columns identify him another way and are asked for by their own wording: drivers.driverRef is the reference name and drivers.url is the introduction website. A question that asks who did something and then asks for one of those keeps the forename and surname and adds that column, since a reference or an address does not say who. A question that already names the driver, or that asks only for the reference names of a set of drivers, returns driverRef on its own. A driver is also called a player, and asking where to know more about him asks for the website. The example joins lapTimes to drivers on driverId and returns the full name and reference name of every driver who set a time on lap 5 of race 350, a race named only by a number being raceId.
sql: SELECT T2.forename, T2.surname, T2.driverRef FROM lapTimes AS T1 INNER JOIN drivers AS T2 ON T2.driverId = T1.driverId WHERE T1.raceId = 350 AND T1.lap = 5

name: Points And Wins From Championship Standings Or From A Single Race
description: driverStandings holds a driver's championship points, wins and position after each race, one row per driver standing in the championship at that point: 25 rows for race 872 where results holds 24, and 32.6 rows a race on average against 24.4. Its points and its wins both accumulate through the season, driver 1 across 2008 reading 10, 14, 14, 20, 28, 38 points while wins climbs 1, 2, 3, 4, so neither is ever summed. Because every row is keyed by a race, naming one Grand Prix only chooses which row to read: a question about a driver's points stays on driverStandings.points whether it names a single race, a whole season or no race at all, and whether it wants a total, an average, a best or the leading few. results.points is the credit for that one race alone. How many drivers took part in a race given only by its number counts the driverStandings rows carrying that raceId. How many times a driver won counts the standings rows where wins is at least one, 3,632 of the 31,578, and never reads points, while his highest points figure is MAX(points). For a constructor the verb decides: points it got, scored or took in a race are per-race figures in constructorResults, while points or wins it has, holds at a given race, or has tallied in total are in constructorStandings. In the example 'German' is a value of constructors.nationality and wins >= 1 keeps the standings rows from the point a win was already banked, the name and points being read from each such row.
sql: SELECT T2.name, T1.points FROM constructorStandings AS T1 INNER JOIN constructors AS T2 ON T1.constructorId = T2.constructorId WHERE T2.nationality = 'German' AND T1.wins >= 1

name: Rank, Position And Final Rank Are Three Different Placings
description: results.rank ranks a driver by his fastest lap inside one race, so rank 1 set the quickest lap and ranking the highest is the smallest number. Anyone said to have ranked first, ranked second or ranked at some number is found by filtering results.rank at that number, constructors exactly as drivers by joining results to constructors on constructorId, and the top ten on that measure are the rows with rank < 11. A top few asked for by points orders the standings instead. A position, which a question may call a track number, is neither the rank nor results.position, a column left empty for every entry that did not finish: a driver's position is driverStandings.position, a constructor's is constructorStandings.position, and a position held during a lap is lapTimes.position. A final rank is the place an entry finished in, results.positionOrder. In the example results.rank = 3 picks the entries that set the third quickest lap of their race and races.year = 2009 confines them to that season, the constructor name and the year being returned for each.
sql: SELECT T2.name, T3.year FROM results AS T1 INNER JOIN constructors AS T2 ON T1.constructorId = T2.constructorId INNER JOIN races AS T3 ON T1.raceId = T3.raceId WHERE T1.rank = 3 AND T3.year = 2009

name: Choosing Whose url Answers A Request For More Information
description: Five tables carry a url, the page for the row they describe: circuits, races, drivers, constructors and seasons. An introduction, information or more information about something, a website or its link, where to know more, a Wiki Pedia page and a season page all name that column. The one to return belongs to the thing the question is scoped by, not to a table joined on the way: races held at a named circuit are scoped by the circuit, so circuits.url answers even though races carry a url of their own, and the season a numbered race fell in is answered by seasons.url. A circuit hosts many races, so the join repeats its single address and the projection is distinct, while a filter pinning one race needs no DISTINCT. In the example 'Monza' is a value of circuits.location, the town of the circuit titled 'Autodromo Nazionale di Monza', and races.year > 2000 compares an integer, keeping the later seasons.
sql: SELECT DISTINCT T1.url FROM circuits AS T1 INNER JOIN races AS T2 ON T2.circuitId = T1.circuitId WHERE T1.location = 'Monza' AND T2.year > 2000

name: When A Race Took Place, And Where Its Place Name Lives
description: When a race happened is races.date and races.time. A full circuit title like 'Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya' is a value of circuits.name, but a place named loosely as a city plus the word circuit usually is not: no circuits.name equals 'Abu Dhabi Circuit', since that circuit is named 'Yas Marina Circuit', and the string survives only as circuits.location = 'Abu Dhabi' and inside races.name = 'Abu Dhabi Grand Prix'. Filtering a column on a string it does not hold returns an empty result rather than an error, so check where the value lives. The example takes that route: circuits.location = 'Abu Dhabi' with races.year = 2012, an integer and so unquoted, pins the single 2012 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix and projects both its date and time, one specific occurrence being a calendar date together with a clock time. A list across several races projects only the attribute asked for, times with DISTINCT because they repeat, dates without. When a season or a round was is answered with races.date, never with the year.
sql: SELECT DISTINCT T2.date, T2.time FROM circuits AS T1 INNER JOIN races AS T2 ON T2.circuitId = T1.circuitId WHERE T2.year = 2012 AND T1.location = 'Abu Dhabi'
